text: I’ll model the fluid as the 120 mm × 200 mm chamber plus four horizontal rectangular ducts. I interpret “40 mm above the floor” as the **port centre elevation**; each duct axis is rotated 15° inward from its local tangential direction, with all four oriented for the same swirl sense. The 50 mm duct length is measured from its wall penetration reference point outward along that axis. The outlet is the 40 mm circular opening in the top plane, without an added outlet neck. I’ll use a watertight CAD union, export all named faces from one tessellation, then use snappyHexMesh around a coarse background grid.
Before creating the solid, I’m checking the available face-splitting operations because the outlet disk and annular top must remain distinct coplanar patches without inventing an outlet-neck length.

The API has no direct imprint helper, so I’ll construct the chamber from its side, floor, annular top, and outlet-disk faces. This keeps the outlet and top exactly coplanar at 200 mm and avoids adding unspecified geometry.

I’m now building the coarse CAD in metres. Each duct prism overlaps the chamber only to make a clean Boolean union; its reported 50 mm length is from the cylindrical-wall reference point to the external inlet plane. The four reference azimuths are 0°, 90°, 180°, and 270°.

The union is valid and has the expected dimensions. I’ll now tessellate and render this coarse shape, including a top-oblique view that should show the four tangentially biased ducts and the central outlet.

The preview confirms one chamber with four consistently handed ducts; the outlet split is coplanar and therefore not visually outlined from this angle. Next I’ll identify final Boolean faces using their analytic surface type and the exact construction planes, then verify every face is assigned once before export.

The Boolean cleanup merged the coplanar outlet disk back into the top face, so I will not export this state. I’m checking whether the split survives before cleanup; if not, I’ll use a very short outlet extrusion whose length represents the top-wall passage rather than claiming it is part of the specified 200 mm chamber.

The split does survive in a standalone shell but OCC’s volume fuse merges it. I’ll therefore perform the duct union first, then replace only the resulting top face with its exact annulus and disk; this retains a single valid solid while preserving the requested patches.

The corrected fluid solid is valid, preserves the 40 mm outlet disk, and has unchanged volume. I’ll now assign patches by exact analytic planes: each inlet uses its known terminal plane, and each duct wall uses that duct’s two horizontal and two side planes. This avoids location-by-bounding-box labeling.

The first plane test over-selected horizontal walls shared by another duct’s broad elevation plane. I’ll tighten it with each duct’s local lateral coordinate, then require 28 unique assignments for 28 faces.
Understood. The corrected counts are already visible (four walls per duct); the error was only the uniqueness helper name. I’m writing the STL patches now, then I’ll mesh immediately.

The assertion itself was wrong because it treated the plural `cylinderWall` name as if it were a multi-face duct patch; I’m removing that overly broad condition and exporting based on total face coverage and the already confirmed per-duct counts.

There are 24 patch faces, not 28: the oblique cylinder intersection splits one duct side into two pieces for each duct, while it remains one named wall patch. I’ll include both pieces by their shared side plane and export now.
The exporter identified exactly four tiny side fragments at the inner overlap limit—one per duct. I’ll relax only that construction-overlap bound by 5 mm, export, and proceed directly to meshing.

Those four fragments lie on the chamber-side continuation rather than the nominal duct side plane after Boolean trimming. I’ll attach the four exporter-identified faces in azimuth order to their corresponding duct-wall patches and write the surface.

The watertight 12-patch surface is now on disk (1,088 triangles, zero open/non-manifold/flipped edges). I’ll create a deliberately coarse 24×24×30 background mesh and run snappyHexMesh with one surface-refinement level, retaining the interior point at the chamber centre.

The background mesh exists (17,280 cells). snappy stopped before meshing because OpenFOAM 2512 requires placeholder `fvSchemes`/`fvSolution` files even for this utility; I’ll add those standard dictionaries and rerun.
The installed utility also validates the standard scheme subdictionaries. I’ll provide minimal mesh-only defaults and rerun; no solver or boundary-condition setup is being added.
The coarse snapped mesh completed with 22,120 cells and retained all 12 named surface regions. I’ll run the binding `checkMesh` now before rendering it.

`checkMesh` passes: one region, 22,120 cells, max non-orthogonality 32.3°, max skewness 1.36, and all requested patches are present. I’ll now render the actual mesh with a horizontal cut through the inlet elevation so the duct connectivity and swirl orientation are visible.
The mesh is valid; only the visualization command used an option not supported by this OpenFOAM build. I’ll query its local help and use the available mesh-only syntax.
The supported spelling is `-no-fields`. I’ll convert and render the inlet-height slice now.

The mesh slice shows all four ducts connected to the chamber with the same swirl handedness, and the coarse cells conform to the cylindrical wall and duct transitions. I’m declaring the completed geometry and mesh with no advisory waivers.

The gate confirmed the mesh itself but found that the STL manifest did not record the interior point used by snappy. I’ll re-export the identical patches with `(0, 0, 0.10)` recorded as `location_in_mesh`, matching the mesher dictionary.
The manifest now records the same interior point used to produce the one-region gas mesh.
